posts.body_html:
some pictures from last spring, they're still very much dormant right now and I just "BEAT THE CRAP" out of them aka ripped out tons of rhizomes from these community mother plant trays. No plants were harmed in the process, despite what appeared to be some gang related activity, although I did bruise my thumb in the process hah! Technically speaking, there was no violence involved, since this neither hurts, kills, or destroys the plants, but dividing can definitely rough up the grower! It's literally like pulling teeth, and even if you're "fat but buff" like MW, it's still not easy.

Pics taken 5/19/23:




Yes, I labeled this one last year, "found it" yesterday amongst the hundreds of growth points, and was able to get one measly division from it.


S. oreophila collection (this includes other populations an clones):


LIDZ view:






literally busting out of the tray! If you don't dig out some rhizomes, they get overcrowded like this and pitchers have to be thinned out to prevent trouble from happening:

posts.body_html: The old summer leaves were removed during the fall, which triggered some plants to produce fall traps! It really doesn't seem to matter which population of oreophila it is, this species in general reacts to light exposure to the growth points, although I'm sure there's more to it than that. Pics taken 10/28/25:
posts.body_text: The old summer leaves were removed during the fall, which triggered some plants to produce fall traps!  It really doesn't seem to matter which population of oreophila it is, this species in general reacts to light exposure to the growth points, although I'm sure there's more to it than that.  Pics taken 10/28/25:

posts.body_html: Out of those few traps that developed late in the season, a few of them colored up! It's interesting because some of them are still green while others are turning red. It makes you wonder if this is genetics or environment. Since everything is equal, are some clones are more "capable" of coloring up than others? Will the green traps eventually turn red because they're just younger and need more time to color up? We'll see. In any case, these characteristics suggest oreophila has some serious breeding potential. Pics taken 12/10/25:
